  <td class="topic"><a href="sessions/02-causality.html">2 · Theory and causality</a>
    <span class="t-desc">A theory is a set of assumptions that produces a prediction you could be wrong about. Empirical work can settle part of that and never all of it. Then causality proper: every comparison stands in for a world that did not happen, and the graph tells you which variables to condition on and which to leave alone.</span></td>
  <td class="hw">Your team's written ground rules — agreed and handed in today</td></tr>
<tr><td>Wed Sep 9</td>
  <td class="topic"><a href="sessions/03-questions.html">3 · Finding the question</a>
    <span class="t-desc">Finding the question is the job, not the preamble to it. Five shapes a good project takes, six ways they go wrong, and a filter of four questions that kills most of the rest. Then the relay, where you break somebody else's question and they break yours.</span></td>
  <td class="hw"></td></tr>
<tr><td>Wed Sep 16</td>
  <td class="topic"><a href="sessions/04-ethics.html">4 · Ethics and access</a>
    <span class="t-desc">Two gates stand between your design and your data, and they are different kinds of thing. The IRB is an ethics review. A data-use agreement is a contract. Both take longer than teams expect, which is why this meeting sits in September rather than in November.</span></td>
  <td class="hw"></td></tr>
<tr class="g-last g02"><td>Wed Sep 23<sup class="resched">*</sup></td>

    <span class="t-desc">Every serious analysis is code, whether or not you wrote it. "Use AI" is four different things and they fail differently — only one of them produces output you can check. Then the practical business of getting a file at all: what Cornell already pays for, what an API is, and why scraping is the last resort dressed up as the clever one.</span></td>
  <td class="hw"></td></tr>

<tr class="g-first g03"><td class="g-rail" rowspan="4"><span>Methods &amp; designs</span></td><td>Wed Sep 30</td>
  <td class="topic"><a href="sessions/06-models-uncertainty.html">6 · Models and uncertainty</a>
    <span class="t-desc">What the standard models estimate, and how to read a coefficient in the units of the problem. Where uncertainty comes from, and what a p-value is not. Then the distinction that decides half your projects: explaining or predicting.</span></td>
  <td class="hw">Project pitch — one page · Exercise 1 — interrogate a dataset, end of week · Rate your teammates</td></tr>
<tr><td>Wed Oct 7</td>
  <td class="topic"><a href="sessions/07-model-failures.html">7 · Model failures</a>
    <span class="t-desc">Estimates fail in two ways. Bias moves the number: selection and sorting, omitted variables, measurement error, reverse causality. False precision leaves the number alone and shrinks the error bar around it. Then the fix everybody reaches for, and its ceiling — 'I added controls' is a claim about the graph, not a technique.</span></td>
  <td class="hw"></td></tr>
<tr><td>Wed Oct 14</td>
  <td class="topic"><a href="sessions/08-designs-i.html">8 · Research designs I</a>
    <span class="t-desc">Experiments, instrumental variables, regression discontinuity. What variation each exploits, what each assumes, and how each fails.</span></td>
  <td class="hw"></td></tr>
<tr class="g-last g03"><td>Wed Oct 21<sup class="resched">*</sup></td>
  <td class="topic"><a href="sessions/09-designs-ii.html">9 · Research designs II</a>
    <span class="t-desc">Difference-in-differences, panel data with fixed effects, event studies. The question is the same each time: which identifying variation survives the fixed effects, and what assumption is left carrying the estimate.</span></td>
  <td class="hw"></td></tr>

<tr class="g-first g04"><td class="g-rail" rowspan="3"><span>Communication</span></td><td>Wed Oct 28</td>

    <span class="t-desc">Writing is taught here, as a method rather than as advice. A piece of writing is built outline first — one topic sentence per paragraph, in order, before any prose exists. The fastest way to see that is backwards.</span></td>
  <td class="hw"></td></tr>
<tr><td>Wed Nov 4</td>

    <span class="t-desc">Which figure answers which question, and why — distributions, time, space, comparison. Then what figures hide: aggregation, scale, binning, projection, area scaled by radius, chosen windows, counts where you needed a rate. Then the hard half nobody practises — an honest figure that still makes a point.</span></td>
  <td class="hw">Writing 1 — reverse outline</td></tr>

    <span class="t-desc">A talk is an outline with pictures. One claim per slide, and the claim is the slide title, not a label. <script>
(function () {
  var now = new Date();
  if (now < new Date(2026, 7, 20) || now > new Date(2026, 11, 9)) return;
  var months = {Jan:0,Feb:1,Mar:2,Apr:3,May:4,Jun:5,Jul:6,Aug:7,Sep:8,Oct:9,Nov:10,Dec:11};
  var today = new Date(now.getFullYear(), now.getMonth(), now.getDate());
  var rows = document.querySelectorAll('.grouped-schedule tbody tr');
  for (var i = 0; i < rows.length; i++) {
    if (rows[i].classList.contains('break-row')) continue;
    var cells = rows[i].cells;
    for (var j = 0; j < cells.length; j++) {
      var m = cells[j].textContent.trim()
        .match(/^(?:Mon|Tue|Wed|Thu|Fri|Sat|Sun) ([A-Z][a-z]{2}) (\d{1,2})\*?$/);
      if (!m) continue;
      if (new Date(2026, months[m[1]], +m[2]) >= today) {
        rows[i].classList.add('next-class');
        cells[j].classList.add('today-cell');
        return;
      }
      break;
    }
  }
})();
</script>
